Bug killers for Hyacinth

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The water hyacinth at Hartbeespoort has plagued the dam for years, but now a controversial new method is being used to eradicate the alien plants. Will it work and are residents onboard?

Unique Selling Point:
The Harties hyacinth, a topic we have covered over the past 10 years in numerous stories from Joy's Harties story, to her one on Metsi Ame project, then I did two stories on Harties which we won environmental awards for showing how dirty the water is. 600 million tonnes of sewage which feeds the hyacinth.
The hyacinth is a South American plant that made its way here... and it suffocates fish etc and stops boats from being able to do anything etc
So there have been many attempts to kill it...Chemicals, Machines that moved everything out, they tried pollution control...
And now they've found the Megamelus scutellaris planthoppers. They are natural enemies of water hyacinth, and are host-specific. The planthopper responds well to mass rearing, reproduces rapidly, and recovers faster after periods of cooler temperatures than some of the other biocontrol agent species, according to the CBC. Importantly, they can be “exceptionally damaging” to water hyacinth. One the plant dies it then sinks. Magalies water are also using the plants in the fertilizer project if we wish to show where these plants go?


Summary:
We will interview local residents about the issue:
Their concerns are about the bugs on land, about the sinking of the hyacinth from the bugs eating it, that the stats are incorrect as to how much its reduced hyacinth and there are questions about if this is the best place to pool resources.

I have interviewed a number of experts on the ground involved with the project: Turns out I managed to speak with several people on the ground and establish the following as well - 1. The bugs seen on land are moggies, not the ones from the project. Moggies may look similar and people have mistaken them for the hoppers, however, the ones from the project are only in the water and only survive while the hyacinth survives. When the hyacinth dies, they die. 2. The hyacinth has a short life span, and so hyacinth has been sinking to the bottom of the dam for years, so whether its sinking from the bugs or sinking naturally - the fact that there hasn't been any changes in the past 20 years due to it sinking - makes it unlikely it will make a detrimental environmental change. 3. There is satellite imagery from SANSA (space agency) showing the hyacinth on the dam over the past several years - it shows the difference from before the bugs and now during. Its very accurate in the numbers that have been quoted in the media in terms of percentage reduction 4. The problem has always been upstream - the amount of waste water coming into the dam is what feeds the hyacinth, the problem with removing it with machinery is that it drops the seeds - so it isn't a solution, its a countermeasure, however, the hyacinth is actually being used as compost because of its high nitrate levels (from comes from the ammonia of poo poo).

Environmentalist Patrick Ganda, 41, mass rears the bugs at Grootvaly Blesbokspruit wetland

Scientists warn that while the insects have been fairly successful in controlling the situation, more needs to be done to treat its cause, which authorities could tackle by tightening regulations on waste water management.
They require the estates around the dam to rear the insects…




Further information:
The project is headed by Centre for Biological Control at Rhodes University - professor Julie Coetzee (attached). Julie completed her PhD at the University of the Witswatersrand in 2003. She has published over 20 studies on this... she started working on biological control agents of water hyacinth in 1998, and has never looked back. Recently she has shifted the focus of her work on floating aquatic plants to submerged and emergent aquatic plants. As we have gained excellent control of the floating species, this new suite of species has taken advantage of these new habitats, threatening indigenous aquatic flora and fauna. Tackling these new problem plants is a challenge, but we will benefit from experience gained elsewhere in controlling these species, as well as pioneering new methods of control for South Africa. Julie is the President of the Entomological Society of Southern Africa.


In their last annual report (https://www.ru.ac.za/media/rhodesuniversity/content/zoologyandentomology/cbc/CBC_Annual_Report_2022_FINAL_epub.pdf) it describes how for the third year in a row, water hyacinth was reduced to less than 5% cover at Hartbeespoort Dam through biological control alone. In 2022, it released nearly 400 000 Megamelus scutellaris from its Waainek mass-rearing facility for water hyacinth control around South Africa, while satellite rearing stations run by citizen scientists have released thousands more onto infested waterways.

So they have these little rearing/ breeding stations around the dam at strategic points - there are 5 of them. one of them is at the Hartbeespoort Boat Club... we can interview Ian Hendrickse. Who we've interviewed before.

The program is managed by biological control programme managed by the department of forestry, fisheries and the environment, however, they haven't been funded by them in 2 years.

Script:


1. Amid luxury golf estates and yachts moored next to mansions, a battle is brewing on the surface of the Hart-beest-poort Dam - between a plant and a bug.


On one side: a water weed…on the other… its natural enemy - a 3mm insect whose only job is to chomp away at it…killing it, one bite at a time.


BREATHE.. change tone into more neutral informative music or water natsound


2. Water hyacinth - [hiya-sinth] on Hartbeespoort dam in the North West has become surprisingly politicised. The plant is fed by sewage pollution in the dam - rich in nutrients, it makes the weed double its mass every two weeks …and its exponential growth has wreaked [reeked] havoc on the local tourism industry.


LINK: (Boat engine getting stuck in hyacinth) We took a boat cruise but we almost got stuck in the hyacinth that’s becoming so common here in harties.


Prof Julie Coetzee runs Rhodes University’s Water Weeds Biocontrol Programme.


Julie: It's a political system there's a lot of people who rely on this damn for businesses there's all these beautiful estates around here and so the policy at the time was to keep water high since a way through herbicidal spray there was no more budgets allocated so by the middle of 2017 the dam was covered with water hyacinth.


3. A decade ago she led a research team to Argentina, where the hyacinth originates from, apparently brought here by people who liked the flowers.

The scientists looked for anything in its native home that could control the weed - a planthopper called Megamellus Scutellaris [mega-mellus scootalaris] showed promise.


We wanted to see it in its new home in Harties where it’s shown single-minded focus.


Govan: You guys have gone to South America to fetch the hopper?

Julie: yeah, these insects can only feed on water hyacinth there's nothing else that they can complete their life cycle on, so they can't lay eggs, they can't develop.


Julie: look look look there's a megamelus with with wings

you see that little guy

Govan: oh my gosh I can't see there oh right

Julie: they're harmless look how cute they are that's the bomb squad


5. Magalies Water, the water board in charge of the dam, says a year ago, the hyacinth covered 50% of Harties - this month it’s down by at least 20%.


Julie: At the end of summer we looking at around 10%, then over winter it's not growing.

Govan: Does that make the Hopper the most effective solution for the hyacinth in harties?

Julie: yes, so we calling it an inundative biocontrol program, so we inundating biocontrol program these plants as frequently as possible.


4. The sap-sucking bug pierces the plant’s cells, making it water-logged - reducing its buoyancy and rotting its leaves. Once they turn brown - the hoppers’ job is done.


LINK: So this is a good example of Megamelus Scutellaris actually does, the hyacinth hopper, you can see the plants are brown – and they're actually dying, and you can see that these other plants are on top of it, means that once the wind blows them apart they’ll sink.


6. Because the hoppers only live for 80 days, Julie’s team set up a breeding programme, with seven satellite stations around the dam, for a year-round supply of bugs that they carry to the hyacinth in buckets.


LINK: It’s fairly simple, a green house, a few tanks, dam water and hyacinth and they’re breeding these hyacinth hoppers all year round, but this is what it takes to keep these off the dam, but the key to success comes from the residents around here tending to them.

.


7. In December alone, the team - with residents volunteering - released 160,000 hoppers on the dam. (show frikkie)


GAP - HYACINTH SOUNDS ETC


statistics, problems with hopper and expansion of project
























blue green algae:

8. If this were merely a good news story about nature providing solutions to nature's problems, it would end here. But, it's far more complex than that. The humble hyacinth hopper is not without its critics! Magalies Water Spokesperson David Magae. [magai]


David: We can wake up tomorrow and there's no hyacinth right but your raw water quality remains a concern. Exactly but our problem has been that sections of the media are purporting the success exclusively to the existence of the hoppers.

Govan: but the hopper played a large role in getting it down to 20%

David: We acknowledge the role of the hopper however it is not only the effort of the hoppers being around here.


9. Magalies Water was given R77 million to fix the dam – the hopper team got none of that. But Magalies Water is more concerned about addressing the source of pollution upstream – the enormous quantities of raw effluent from dysfunctional sewage plants, and industries, illegally flooding the rivers that feed into the dam …and that feeds the hyacinth.


David: This water comes from Gauteng right

Govan: This is the dirtiest

David: yes?

Govan: But people swim and fish here! The history of this dam is tourism.

Govan: So this is the dirtiest water in the country?

David: yeah yeah now


10. Magalies Water’s Professor Vhahangwele Masindi oversees their water quality lab tests… in the rivers upstream from the dam… to pinpoint polluters.


Polluters are supposed to face fines and even imprisonment, but the Professor is reluctant to name names.


Prof Masingi: Actually what is not happening is an enforcement and also monitoring is not taking place, which is our biggest challenge.

Govan: Which municipalities?

Dr Masingi: I wouldn't be specific

Govan:I can guess if you want okay, the city of Joburg?

the city of Joburg upstream with.

Tshwane? yes

Northern works? yes

Madibeng? yes, they have a wastewater treatment facility.

Did I miss any?

Dr Masingi: no I think you have covered everything


11. In other words, it's up to local municipalities to police the pollution and - because they're failing- Harties is paying the price.


Govan: why don't you just take these guys to court?

Dr Masingi: enforcement lies with the office of the minister


12. Magalies Water has handed this evidence to the Department of Water and Sanitation. To date no city officials, WASTEWATER MANAGERS or COMPANY DIRECTORS have ever been charged.

confront w magalies water










GRAPHIC OF BUBBLES TECH TO COME FROM COMPANY





















MAP OF UP STREAM

13. But magalies Water has a plan.


Prof Masingi: We want to maintain it at less than 5% in this three years. We have tailored an integrated system or technology or pack of technologies that we believe they will turn around the situation that we're experiencing here in a dam.


14. They awarded several tenders: One is for litter traps to catch rubbish coming down the rivers…to be installed in the next few months.

Another is Nanobubble technology - pure oxygen injected into the water to cleanse it. Tests in a much smaller dam showed great success within months.

Possibly the most controversial project is the removing of the hyacinth by hand or machine and turning it into fertiliser. Great for jobs…the only snag is that pollution makes the hyacinth potentially toxic.


Masingi: The good thing about it is that we take the hyacinth and we use it for the production of fertilisers well it means there's an economy is that really good it's very good because

Govan: but the dam has heavy metals in it and then that stays behind in the compost is that really good for people?

Masingi: We yeah we not really sure but I believe because they are certified, the product has been tested and is compliant with the regulatory framework


15. Magalies Water would only consider funding the hoppers if Julie can address their questions about the layer of dead plant matter at the bottom of the dam… once the hyacinth sinks.



Julie: As they get waterlogged they push down and they get heavy and the plant it sinks

Govan: Surely that's not good either?

Julie: These plants are going to sink anyway, we are dealing with the symptom, we are not dealing with the cause, no one's focusing on what, percentage of what's at the bottom of this dam is composed of water hyacinth and all the stuff that's coming in from Joburg.


(show project)

16. But even if the hoppers win the looming showdown, the plan is not to completely eradicate hyacinth - just to keep it under control… because in this toxic ecosystem, it helps control the poisonous, cancer-causing blue-green algae underneath it.

Of course, if the water quality improves, this potentially greater risk might go away.


And perhaps that's the best the residents can hope for. (i mean we need to end it more dramatically…)

They awarded several tenders: One is for litter traps to catch rubbish coming down the rivers…to be installed in the next few months. Masingi: We yeah we not really sure but I believe because they are certified, the product has been tested and is compliant with the regulatory framework 15. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The water hyacinth at Hartbeespoort has plagued the dam for years, but now a controversial new method is being used to eradicate the alien plants. Will it work and are residents onboard?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Harties hyacinth, a topic we have covered over the past 10 years in numerous stories from Joy's Harties story, to her one on Metsi Ame project, then I did two stories on Harties which we won environmental awards for showing how dirty the water is. 600 million tonnes of sewage which feeds the hyacinth. The hyacinth is a South American plant that made its way here... and it suffocates fish etc and stops boats from being able to do anything etc So there have been many attempts to kill it...Chemicals, Machines that moved everything out, they tried pollution control... And now they've found the Megamelus scutellaris planthoppers. They are natural enemies of water hyacinth, and are host-specific. The planthopper responds well to mass rearing, reproduces rapidly, and recovers faster after periods of cooler temperatures than some of the other biocontrol agent species, according to the CBC. Importantly, they can be “exceptionally damaging” to water hyacinth. One the plant dies it then sinks. Magalies water are also using the plants in the fertilizer project if we wish to show where these plants go?
metadata.Summary: We will interview local residents about the issue: Their concerns are about the bugs on land, about the sinking of the hyacinth from the bugs eating it, that the stats are incorrect as to how much its reduced hyacinth and there are questions about if this is the best place to pool resources. I have interviewed a number of experts on the ground involved with the project: Turns out I managed to speak with several people on the ground and establish the following as well - 1. The bugs seen on land are moggies, not the ones from the project. Moggies may look similar and people have mistaken them for the hoppers, however, the ones from the project are only in the water and only survive while the hyacinth survives. When the hyacinth dies, they die. 2. The hyacinth has a short life span, and so hyacinth has been sinking to the bottom of the dam for years, so whether its sinking from the bugs or sinking naturally - the fact that there hasn't been any changes in the past 20 years due to it sinking - makes it unlikely it will make a detrimental environmental change. 3. There is satellite imagery from SANSA (space agency) showing the hyacinth on the dam over the past several years - it shows the difference from before the bugs and now during. Its very accurate in the numbers that have been quoted in the media in terms of percentage reduction 4. The problem has always been upstream - the amount of waste water coming into the dam is what feeds the hyacinth, the problem with removing it with machinery is that it drops the seeds - so it isn't a solution, its a countermeasure, however, the hyacinth is actually being used as compost because of its high nitrate levels (from comes from the ammonia of poo poo). Environmentalist Patrick Ganda, 41, mass rears the bugs at Grootvaly Blesbokspruit wetland Scientists warn that while the insects have been fairly successful in controlling the situation, more needs to be done to treat its cause, which authorities could tackle by tightening regulations on waste water management. They require the estates around the dam to rear the insects…
metadata.Further information: The project is headed by Centre for Biological Control at Rhodes University - professor Julie Coetzee (attached). Julie completed her PhD at the University of the Witswatersrand in 2003. She has published over 20 studies on this... she started working on biological control agents of water hyacinth in 1998, and has never looked back. Recently she has shifted the focus of her work on floating aquatic plants to submerged and emergent aquatic plants. As we have gained excellent control of the floating species, this new suite of species has taken advantage of these new habitats, threatening indigenous aquatic flora and fauna. Tackling these new problem plants is a challenge, but we will benefit from experience gained elsewhere in controlling these species, as well as pioneering new methods of control for South Africa. Julie is the President of the Entomological Society of Southern Africa. In their last annual report (https://www.ru.ac.za/media/rhodesuniversity/content/zoologyandentomology/cbc/CBC_Annual_Report_2022_FINAL_epub.pdf) it describes how for the third year in a row, water hyacinth was reduced to less than 5% cover at Hartbeespoort Dam through biological control alone. In 2022, it released nearly 400 000 Megamelus scutellaris from its Waainek mass-rearing facility for water hyacinth control around South Africa, while satellite rearing stations run by citizen scientists have released thousands more onto infested waterways. So they have these little rearing/ breeding stations around the dam at strategic points - there are 5 of them. one of them is at the Hartbeespoort Boat Club... we can interview Ian Hendrickse. Who we've interviewed before. The program is managed by biological control programme managed by the department of forestry, fisheries and the environment, however, they haven't been funded by them in 2 years.
